title: Metric Space Definition and Standard Metrics
oneLine: A metric space is a set equipped with a distance function satisfying positivity, symmetry, and triangle inequality.
statement:
A metric space is a pair $(X, d)$ where $X$ is a non-empty set and $d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a function (called a metric or distance) satisfying for all $x, y, z \in X$:

(1) Positivity: $d(x, y) \ge 0$, and $d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y$.

(2) Symmetry: $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$.

(3) Triangle Inequality: $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

Standard examples include Euclidean metric $d_2(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2}$, taxicab $d_1(x, y) = \sum |x_i - y_i|$, Chebyshev $d_\infty(x, y) = \max |x_i - y_i|$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the discrete metric ($d(x, y) = 1$ if $x \ne y$), and the uniform metric $d_\infty(f, g) = \sup_{t \in [a, b]} |f(t) - g(t)|$ on $C[a, b]$.
intuition:
In Real Analysis I, distance was always the 1D absolute value difference $|x - y|$. Metric spaces liberate analysis from the real line, letting us measure distances between vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, continuous functions, sequences, or matrices!

The three rules ensure that distance behaves like physical distance: it is never negative, distance zero means same location, direction does not alter distance, and a detour cannot be shorter than the straight line.
traps: Forgetting that $d(x, y) = 0 \implies x = y$. Functions that satisfy everything except this are only *pseudometrics*.
The discrete metric makes EVERY subset both open and closed! Never assume metric spaces share all topological quirks of $\mathbb{R}$.

cards.q: State the three axioms that define a metric $d$ on a set $X$.
cards.a: (1) $d(x, y) \ge 0$ with equality iff $x = y$; (2) $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$; (3) $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

cards.q: What is the discrete metric on a set $X$?
cards.a: $d(x, y) = 0$ if $x = y$, and $d(x, y) = 1$ if $x \ne y$.

title: Open Balls and Open Sets in Metric Spaces
oneLine: An open ball is the interior of a sphere; open sets are arbitrary unions of open balls.
statement:
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space.

(a) The open ball of radius $r > 0$ centered at $x_0 \in X$ is: $$B(x_0, r) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) < r\}$$

(b) A subset $U \subseteq X$ is open if for every $x \in U$, there exists $r > 0$ such that $B(x, r) \subseteq U$.

(c) The empty set $\emptyset$ and whole space $X$ are open; arbitrary unions of open sets are open; finite intersections of open sets are open.
intuition:
Open sets are sets with 'wiggle room': wherever you stand inside an open set, you can take a small step in ANY direction without falling out of the set.

In $\mathbb{R}$, an open ball is just an open interval $(x_0 - r, x_0 + r)$. In $\mathbb{R}^2$, it is a circular disk without its boundary circle.
traps: Infinite intersections of open sets need NOT be open! For example, $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1/n) = \{0\}$, which is closed, not open.
An open ball in the discrete metric with radius $r \le 1$ is just a single point $\{x_0\}$, so every singleton is open!

cards.q: Define an open ball $B(x_0, r)$ in a metric space $(X, d)$.
Is an arbitrary intersection of open sets guaranteed to be open?
cards.a: No, only finite intersections are guaranteed to be open (e.g. $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1/n) = \{0\}$).

title: Closed Sets, Limit Points, and Closure
oneLine: A set is closed iff it contains all its limit points; its closure is the set plus its boundary points.
statement:
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space and $E \subseteq X$.

(a) A point $x \in X$ is a limit point (cluster point) of $E$ if every open ball $B(x, r)$ contains a point $y \in E$ with $y \ne x$. The set of limit points is denoted $E'$.

(b) $E$ is closed if its complement $X \setminus E$ is open. Equivalently, $E$ is closed if and only if $E' \subseteq E$ (it contains all its limit points).

(c) The closure of $E$ is $\overline{E} = E \cup E'$. It is the smallest closed set containing $E$.
intuition: Think of limit points as points that can be snuck up on from inside $E$. A set is closed if no outsider can sneak in through a back door—every boundary point already belongs to the set.
traps: Sets are NOT like doors: a set can be BOTH open and closed (clopen), such as $\emptyset$ and $X$, or NEITHER open nor closed (like $[0, 1)$).
An isolated point of $E$ is in $E$ but is NOT a limit point of $E$.

proof.idea: Show $X \setminus E$ is open iff $E$ contains every limit point.
proof.why: If an outsider $x \notin E$ were a limit point, every ball around $x$ would hit $E$, preventing $X \setminus E$ from containing any ball around $x$.

rungs.why: (=>) Suppose $E$ is closed, so $U = X \setminus E$ is open. Let $x \in E'$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A limit point has points of $E$ crowding arbitrarily close to it from all sides.

rungs.why: If $x \notin E$, then $x \in U$. Since $U$ is open, there is $r > 0$ with $B(x, r) \subseteq U = X \setminus E$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If $x$ were outside the closed set, it would have an open safety bubble that never touches $E$.

rungs.why: This directly contradicts that $x$ is a limit point of $E$. Therefore, $x \in E$, proving $E' \subseteq E$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The safety bubble and the limit point condition cannot coexist; hence every limit point must already belong to $E$.

rungs.why: (<=) Conversely, assume $E' \subseteq E$. Let $x \in X \setminus E$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since all limit points are inside $E$, any outsider is disqualified from being a limit point.

rungs.why: Since $x$ is not a limit point, there exists $r > 0$ such that $B(x, r) \cap E = \emptyset$, meaning $B(x, r) \subseteq X \setminus E$. Thus $X \setminus E$ is open.
rungs.m: $$B(x, r) \subseteq X \setminus E \implies X \setminus E \text{ is open} \implies E \text{ is closed}$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Every outsider has its own personal bubble staying clear of $E$, proving the complement is open and $E$ is closed.

proof.ends: A subset of a metric space is closed if and only if it contains all its limit points.

cards.q: What is the relationship between closed sets and limit points in a metric space?
cards.a: A set is closed if and only if it contains all of its limit points ($E' \subseteq E$).

cards.q: Define the closure $\overline{E}$ of a set $E$.
cards.a: $\overline{E} = E \cup E'$, which is the intersection of all closed sets containing $E$.

title: Convergence of Sequences in Metric Spaces
oneLine: A sequence converges to x iff the real distance d(x_n, x) shrinks to 0.
statement:
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space.

(a) A sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$ converges to $x \in X$ (written $x_n \to x$ or $\lim x_n = x$) if: $$\forall \varepsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} : n \ge K \implies d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon$$

(b) Uniqueness: Limits in a metric space are always unique.

(c) Sequential Characterization of Closed Sets: A set $E \subseteq X$ is closed if and only if for every sequence $(x_n)$ in $E$ with $x_n \to x \in X$, the limit $x$ belongs to $E$.
intuition:
Convergence in an abstract metric space simply reduces to real sequence convergence: $(x_n) \to x$ in $X$ means the real numbers $d(x_n, x) \to 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

A closed set is a 'trap': if your points walk around inside $E$ and converge to a target, that target must remain inside $E$.
traps: In the discrete metric, a sequence converges if and only if it is EVENTUALLY CONSTANT ($x_n = x$ for all large $n$).
Confusing convergence in $C[a, b]$ under $d_\infty$ (which is uniform convergence) with pointwise convergence.

proof.idea: Use the triangle inequality to prove uniqueness, and use open balls to connect sequential limits to closed sets.
proof.why: If $x_n \to x$ and $x_n \to y$, then $d(x, y) \le d(x, x_n) + d(x_n, y) < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$, forcing $d(x, y) = 0$.

rungs.why: For uniqueness, suppose $x_n \to x$ and $x_n \to y$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K_1, K_2$ so $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon/2$ and $d(x_n, y) < \varepsilon/2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Once $n$ is large enough, the sequence is within $\varepsilon/2$ of both candidate limits simultaneously.

rungs.why: Apply the Triangle Inequality to $d(x, y)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The distance between the two targets cannot exceed the sum of their distances to the intermediate term.

rungs.why: Since $d(x, y) < \varepsilon$ for EVERY $\varepsilon > 0$, by Theorem 2.1.9 we must have $d(x, y) = 0$, so $x = y$.
rungs.m: $$\forall \varepsilon > 0, \; 0 \le d(x, y) < \varepsilon \implies d(x, y) = 0 \implies x = y$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Two points separated by a distance smaller than any positive number must be the exact same point.

proof.ends: Limits in any metric space are unique, and closed sets are precisely those closed under sequential limits.

cards.q: What does $x_n \to x$ mean in a metric space $(X, d)$?
cards.a: For every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge K$.

cards.q: Characterize closed sets in terms of sequences.
cards.a: $E$ is closed iff whenever $(x_n) \subseteq E$ converges to $x$, the limit $x \in E$.

title: Continuity of Mappings Between Metric Spaces
oneLine: A mapping is continuous iff the inverse image of every open set is open.
statement:
Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces, and $f: X \to Y$.

(a) $f$ is continuous at $c \in X$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that: $$d_X(x, c) < \delta \implies d_Y(f(x), f(c)) < \varepsilon$$

(b) Global Topological Criterion: $f$ is continuous on $X$ if and only if for every open set $V \subseteq Y$, the pre-image $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$.

(c) Equivalently, $f$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(F)$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $F \subseteq Y$.
intuition:
The topological definition $f^{-1}(\text{open}) = \text{open}$ is the crown jewel of modern analysis: it eliminates $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ completely!

Continuous maps preserve proximity: pulling back a neighborhood of an image point gives a neighborhood of the original point.
traps: The FORWARD image of an open set $f(U)$ does NOT have to be open! (e.g. constant function $f(x) = 0$ sends open interval $(-1, 1)$ to singleton $\{0\}$, which is closed).
Continuity requires pulling BACK open sets, never pushing forward.

proof.idea: Show the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ ball definition translates directly to pre-images of open sets.
proof.why: A point $c \in f^{-1}(V)$ means $f(c) \in V$. Since $V$ is open, it contains an $\varepsilon$-ball; continuity pulls this back to a $\delta$-ball around $c$ inside $f^{-1}(V)$.

rungs.why: (=>) Assume $f$ is continuous and $V \subseteq Y$ is open. Take any $c \in f^{-1}(V)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Picking a point in the pre-image means its output lands safely inside $V$.

rungs.why: Since $V$ is open, choose $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $B_Y(f(c), \varepsilon) \subseteq V$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Inside the open target set $V$, the output point has an open buffer zone.

rungs.why: By continuity of $f$ at $c$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $d_X(x, c) < \delta \implies d_Y(f(x), f(c)) < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Continuity guarantees a tiny input bubble whose entire image stays inside that target buffer zone.

rungs.why: Taking pre-images gives $B_X(c, \delta) \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$, proving $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since every point in the pre-image has its own open input bubble inside the pre-image, the pre-image is open!

rungs.why: (<=) Conversely, if pre-images of open sets are open, for any $c$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, the open ball $V = B_Y(f(c), \varepsilon)$ is open, so its pre-image is open, yielding a $\delta$-ball around $c$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The open pre-image immediately supplies the required $\delta$-radius for any given $\varepsilon$.

proof.ends: A function between metric spaces is continuous if and only if pre-images of open sets are open.

cards.q: State the global topological characterization of continuity.
cards.a: A map $f: X \to Y$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every open set $V \subseteq Y$.

cards.q: Does a continuous function always map open sets to open sets?
cards.a: No, forward images of open sets need not be open; only inverse images of open sets are guaranteed open.
